q: But beef is rare within these oxless isles; / Goat's flesh there is, no doubt, and kid, and mutton [...].

e: From Middle English *oxeslyppe, from Old English oxanslyppe (“oxlip”), from oxan, genitive of oxa (“ox”) + slyppe (“paste, slimy substance”). Compare cowslip, of similar formation.

q: Well! Had you no shame, you miserable beast, to let such an affront get past your lips? Where you outdo me, I have no idea; for I'm as fit as you for any task, you poor, ill-fated, nonsense-talking oxling.
2003, Nick Nicholas, George Baloglou, An Entertaining Tale of Quadrupeds:

e: From ox + land, in reference to ploughing capacity.
